purpose: Computational-cost characterisation for the discussion section. Captured 6 Aug 2026; not yet decided whether it enters the paper.

gpu_assessment.verdict: GPU acceleration would not help and would most likely be slower.
reasons: Per-call arrays are tiny: 49 agents against ~6-vertex polygons. Kernel launch overhead (5-20 us, several kernels per call) exceeds the arithmetic it would replace.
The integrator is sequential: semi-implicit Euler makes step n+1 depend on step n, so there is no timestep parallelism.
No CUDA device is present; the discrete GPU is AMD and PyTorch is not installed.
Parallelism is already exploited on the correct axis -- independent trials run concurrently across CPU workers.
gpu_assessment.theoretical_alternative: Batching many trials as tensors (e.g. 1000 x 49 agents) would amortise launch overhead, but requires re-implementing the engine with batched semantics in torch or JAX. That is a separate validated-infrastructure project, not an optimisation, and would break bit-exact agreement with the MATLAB reference.

optimisation_available.finding: np.roll is called 497,280 times per trial (27% of runtime), recomputing an unchanging polygon edge rotation every call.
optimisation_available.estimated_gain: ~1.5-2x on CPU by precomputing polygon edges once per scenario.
optimisation_available.why_not_applied: Any change to compute_forces invalidates the cross-language validation chain: bit-exact MATLAB agreement, archived hashes, and the verify_confirm gate. Completed studies would need re-running for consistency. Not worth re-validating the foundation mid-write.

recommended_scaling: More CPU cores. A 32-64 core machine gives 3-6x with no code change and preserves determinism exactly.

reportable_scale_figures.orca_responsive: slower again; RVO2 solves every step for every pedestrian
